cells.tense: You are in the middle of this and you are not looking away.
cells.ask: Name the thing that ended and one thing you're keeping from it — a sentence each, to one person, this week.
cells.core:
Something ended and you're the one in the room with everybody's feelings. You're not hurrying anyone past it. You're not pretending it didn't happen either. You stay in contact while it closes, and that's what lets the next thing actually start.

What you have right now is steadiness that doesn't cost you yourself. You can sit with the mess — the anger, the relief, the guilt that shouldn't be there — and you don't make it worse by fixing it early. The care you're giving is doing real work. Add one thing to it: a structure underneath, something that will still be there next month. You don't need more feeling. You need one steady place to put it.
cells.sheetLine: You're in the room while it ends, and not looking away.
cells.verb: holding the feeling of a room while it ends
cells.place: the clearing that comes after something has finally stopped

cells.tense: You are bracing for an ending that hasn't happened yet and may not need to.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're carrying for someone else and give it back — say the words out loud this week.
cells.core:
You're carrying the ending before it's real. You can feel how it's going to go, and you're already managing it — managing the people, managing the fallout, making room for feelings nobody has had yet. Some of what you call holding is really bracing, and it costs you the thing it was for.

The attunement is real. The anticipation has taken over it. You're so far ahead of the actual moment that the people in the room don't get you — they get your forecast. Hand one burden back to its owner. Not forever. One thing, one day. Endings don't need a manager. They need someone who will still be there when they arrive.

cells.tense: You were in a room where something ended and you stepped out of it.
cells.ask: Tell one person one true thing about how you felt then — past tense, no fixing, and let them hear it unsoftened.
cells.core:
Something ended and you went quiet. Not cold — you're not cold — but you left while staying in the room. You stopped letting the feelings through, and it worked: you got through without being taken apart. The trade is that you're not in contact with anyone now, not in the way you were.

Feeling isn't the shortage. You have plenty. What's thin is contact with what you actually think about it — what's true for you, said plainly, without first guessing what someone wants to hear. That calm certainty is still in there; it just hasn't been asked anything in a while. Start small. One honest sentence to one person, and let the answer be whatever it is.

cells.tense: You are already the one holding this ending, and you'd call it just being practical.
cells.ask: Say out loud once, "I'm the one holding this together" — about one ending you're managing alone.
cells.core:
You're the one taking people through something that ended. You check in. You take the worst of it. You keep the room from falling apart — and if someone asked, you'd say you were just being sensible about a hard time. The care is running, and it's running under the name of logistics.

The gift in this is that you can see the shape of a thing clearly once you stop calling it practical. That clarity isn't extra work — it's the truth underneath the work you've taken on. Name one ending you've been managing without saying so. Not to whoever is in it with you. To one person. The claim is owed, not the care.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person is specifically holding space for a particular ending in their life — the status describes how one capacity operates in a moment, not a biography. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not in the middle of an ending, I'm just tired' and the read would still be about how they meet shifts in general. The ask survives being wrong because it's an observable act of turning toward one person, not a demand to feel a particular thing about a loss. The sentence that serves me more than the person is any line that implies I know what they lost; I've cut that.
